Photograph: Loïc Venance/AFP/Getty Images France French students and police clash as school blockades turn violent More than 200 arrested while teachers join protest over class sizes, exhausting timetables and staff shortages Kim Willsher in Paris Tue 29 Sep 2026 11.19 EDT Last modified on Tue 29 Sep 2026 11.42 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google French teenagers blockading their schools in protest at class sizes, teacher shortages and long timetables have clashed with police, as politicians traded verbal blows over how to respond. Demonstrations that began in Paris last week have escalated and spread across France, with the authorities reporting the arrests of 164 people on Monday. On Tuesday, high school pupils in Lille, northern France, set fire to dustbins and threw bottles, paving stones and other projectiles at police, who responded with teargas after protesters vandalised bus shelters and advertising hoardings. There were confrontations between children and police in Bordeaux, Rennes and Nantes in western France, and Marseille in the south. At the Lamartine lycée, in the north of Paris, students waved placards complaining they had exhausting timetables. One read: “8am-6pm. More hours of lessons than sleep.” On Monday, the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said protests had broken out at 180 schools, and 12 officers, 12 students and three school staff had been injured. By midday on Tuesday, the education ministry was reporting protests at 300 high schools, a further 40 arrests and that 10 students and staff had been injured. View image in fullscreen Students face police at Baggio high school, Lille, on Tuesday. Photograph: Jean-François Badias/AP The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said earlier that escalating the demonstrations would be “irresponsible”. He posted on X: “Fireworks, fires, violence near high schools: nothing justifies endangering students staff or police.” Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI), responded to ministers’ instructions to police, posting on X on Monday: “The high school students protesting are harmless. The Lecornu government has ordered a crackdown. This brutality is irresponsible and has a clear racist undertone. Hands off our youth. Elected officials and France Unbowed activists, step in wherever you can.” Lecornu, responding on X, called Mélenchon’s intervention an “irresponsible escalation”. “The duty of an elected official of the republic is to protect young people and call for calm. Exploiting their anger for partisan purposes is wrong,” he wrote. He added that Mélenchon’s accusation of racism was “an insult”. View image in fullscreen Students blockade the entrance to Hélène Boucher school in Paris on Tuesday. Photograph: Paoloni Jeremy/Abaca/Shutterstock The protests came as French unions went on strike over the government’s budget plans, which include €54m in public spending cuts. Many public sector workers stopped work on Tuesday, including an estimated 40% of primary school teachers. Ryad Rani, president of the Union Syndicale Lycéene (the high school students’ union) had called for a total blockade of France’s high schools as a parallel action but urged protesters to “remain peaceful”. He said the union was protesting about a “general lack of resources, overcrowded classrooms of sometimes 32-35 students and the shortage of teachers and staff”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion He said a circular sent by the interior and the education ministries to the police, telling them to maintain public order outside high schools “with a proportionate use of force”, was a “absolute scandal”. View image in fullscreen Students join a general protest in Paris on Tuesday against the release of next year’s draft budget. Photograph: Teresa Suárez/AP “We’re talking about pupils of 15-18 years old and the government’s only response is automatic and institutionalised repression. It’s unacceptable. High school pupils are taking action to demand fairer and more equitable conditions and they’re being met with the BAC [anti-criminal brigade] and the CRS [riot police],” Rani said. He added that some teachers and school staff had stood in front of students to protect them from police. “Those are the images you should be showing,” Rani told BFM TV. Caroline Chevé, secretary general of the main teachers’ union the Fédération Syndicale Unitaire (FSU – Unitary Trade Union Federation), who joined protesters at a march in central Paris on Tuesday, said she understood pupils’ frustration. “They’re facing the same challenges as we are. They’re in overcrowded classrooms. Sometimes they don’t have enough teachers because of staffing shortages. They see the same reality as we do, and they’re angry,” Chevé said. https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/o.text: Just 47 of the 2,189 books published for under-10s in 2025 featured a Black main character, Photograph: MBI/Alamy View image in fullscreen Just 47 of the 2,189 books published for under-10s in 2025 featured a Black main character, Photograph: MBI/Alamy Children and teenagers Children’s books with Black main characters down 8% in a year, study shows Only 150 of 2,189 titles published in UK for young children last year focused on minority ethnic, disabled or neurodivergent characters Emma Loffhagen Sun 4 Oct 2026 19.01 EDT Last modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 19.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The number of children’s books featuring Black main characters fell by almost 8% last year, according to research into diversity in UK publishing. Just 47 – or 2.1% – of the 2,189 books published for under-10s in 2025 featured a Black main character, a 7.8% fall from the previous year, according to Inclusive Books for Children. Black children make up about 8.5% of that age bracket in England and Wales. Representation of south Asian main characters fell by 14.3 percentage points to 1.4%, despite children of south Asian heritage making up about 12.4% of the population of under-10s. Just three books featured main characters of Middle Eastern and North African (MENA) heritage, down 50% from the previous year. This represented 0.1% of surveyed books, compared with the group’s 2.2% share of the population. The research by the literacy charity found that only 150 books – 6.9% of those surveyed – featured main characters from minority ethnic, disabled or neurodivergent backgrounds. Of these, 37.3% were written or illustrated by creators who did not share the background of their characters. View image in fullscreen The author Sheena Patel says children need books ‘that reflect both the lives they live and the ones they don’t’. Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The Observer The author Sheena Patel said: “At an age when children are figuring out the world around them and where they fit in, it’s vital they have access to funny, inspiring, adventurous books that reflect both the lives they live and the ones they don’t. We must do better.” The report surveyed baby and toddler books, picture books and fiction for children aged up to nine. It found that representation of disabled characters in picture books fell sharply: the number with disabled main characters dropped by 60% in 2025, to just two titles. Neither was by a disabled creator. The survey also highlighted what it described as a lack of “incidental representation”: stories in which a main character’s identity does not explicitly drive the plot of the story. Dr Stella Louis, an early years consultant, trainer and author, pointed to this “continued reliance” on books where identity itself was the story. “Why can’t a child simply be south Asian, disabled, neurodivergent or bilingual and also be the hero of an ordinary story about friendship, adventure, loss or joy?” she said. The report found that all three books published in 2025 with MENA main characters were refugee narratives. The study authors said children of MENA heritage needed stories covering a broader range of themes and experiences. “As an Arab author, it is painful to see the number of children’s fiction books representing our region decline from six to only three in 2025,” said Nadine Kaadan. She said the fact that all three books published were focused on refugee experiences risked reinforcing a “single story” about the region, defining it through “war and displacement rather than our rich cultures and heritage”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Bookmarks Discover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to you after newsletter promotion There were some signs of progress. Neurodivergent representation increased in picture books, from three titles in 2024 to 13 last year. In the baby and toddler category, the number of books with marginalised main characters rose by 29.4%. Jack Hope, a children’s book consultant, said: “When children’s enjoyment of reading is at a significant low, it’s more important than ever that the stories children encounter reflect their lives, identities, experiences and emotions. “These figures need to be more than mere statistics and a call to action for continued change and improvements.” Explore more on these topics Children and teenagers Publishing Race Black British culture news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story England’s teenagers outperform peers in most countries in maths, reading and science Schools in England sidelining dressing-up for World Book Day, MPs hear Only 10% of boys aged 14-16 read daily for pleasure, National Literacy Trust finds Children’s vocabulary shrinking as reading loses out to screen time, says Susie Dent Susie Dent’s tips and tricks to add muscle to a child’s vocabulary Is listening to an audiobook as good as reading? https://www.theguardian.com/technology/l.text: Jensen Huang is expected to testify before the US Congress in the next fortnight, after the Nvidia CEO stepped down from the multi-trillion dollar company on Thursday, plunging the chipmaker into crisis and sending shock waves across the global AI industry. House foreign affairs chair Brian Mast, a Florida Republican, told reporters on Thursday that congressional staff spoke to Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for Huang’s testimony. Mast and two other leading House Republicans asked Huang last week to brief them behind closed doors about his relationship with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy. Huang has denied any knowledge that Alice Huang allegedly worked for the Chinese government. The pair were seen together around the world, dining in restaurants and attending meetings, over the past few years.
